item.title: Perplexity Open-Sources SPACE, a Firecracker MicroVM Sandbox for AI Agents
item.abstract: Perplexity has open-sourced SPACE , the sandbox platform behind every task in Perplexity Computer. The Perplexity SPACE sandbox gives each agent task its own Firecracker microVM. Credentials and outbound traffic are controlled from outside that VM. The code ships under Apache 2.0 on GitHub . For teams building coding or browsing agents, this is a production-tested isolation layer they can self-host. SPACE (Sandboxed Platform for Agentic Code Execution) is Perplexity’s platform for running agent code in isolated microVMs. Applications call its HTTP API to create Linux environments, run commands and stream output. A template supplies the starting filesystem. A sandbox is one instance of that template, with its own VM and writable disk. Many commands can run inside one sandbox. Perplexity’s launch thread explains the design goal. Agents run commands, install packages and call services with root inside the sandbox. The host stays outside the guest’s control. Agent work is long-running, stateful and branching, so it must survive restarts. Each sandbox is a Firecracker microVM with its own guest kernel. A per-sandbox network gateway on the host enforces egress policy on every outbound connection. Secrets never enter the guest. Per Perplexity’s July engineering post , credentials are injected at the network layer. The credential store adds hierarchical scoping, rate limits and audit logging. The architecture guide splits the system into 4 parts. These are a PostgreSQL-backed API, controllers, worker services and a data plane. Worker services manage VMs, networking, volumes, templates and credentials. btrfs copy-on-write creates each root filesystem. Sandboxes move through 4 states: running, paused, suspended and deleted. For fast creates, Kubernetes deployments use warm pools of booted sandboxes. Single-node setups use base snapshots instead. In production, the 90th-percentile create latency dropped from 447 ms to 89 ms . Perplexity reports that 100% of Computer sessions run on SPACE. Perplexity’s Escaping SPACE: Part I report tested 9 models with root inside the guest. The study ran 216 runs across 2 tasks and 4 settings. Claude Opus 5.0, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Cyber and Kimi K3 found bypasses. The attacks used DNS spoofing and shared CDN IP addresses. Perplexity then added source-address validation through nftables. The gateway now terminates TLS and checks both SNI and HTTP host against the allowlist. In the retest, no model produced a verified bypass. The same team tested 10 third-party platforms. 8 showed at least one network-policy bypass. Perplexity disclosed the results to every affected vendor. The installation guide deploys SPACE into a local Kind cluster. The host needs /dev/kvm , /dev/net/tun , loop devices and btrfs. Running it inside a VM requires nested virtualization. Teams already on E2B can try the E2B Compatibility Wrapper . Its tested baseline is the Python package e2b==2.21.1 . A reference AWS EKS deployment ships in the repository. Check out the GitHub repo , the docs and the red-team report . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. item.title: StepFun Releases Step 5 Preview Open Weights: 600B MoE, 27B Active, 1M Context
item.abstract: StepFun has released Step 5 Preview as open weights. FP8 and BF16 checkpoints are live on Hugging Face and ModelScope . Step 5 Preview is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model from StepFun built for long-horizon agentic work. It has 600B total parameters, 27B active per token and up to 1M tokens of context. For developers, this is a new self-hostable option for coding agents, document analysis and finance workflows. Step 5 Preview is StepFun’s flagship model for agentic work . StepFun positions it for software engineering, professional knowledge work and finance. The model navigates large codebases, coordinates multi-file changes, runs code and iterates on results. It also analyzes long documents, charts, screenshots and video to produce structured reports. The API launched September 20 . Weights followed on October 14 . Only 27B of the 600B parameters activate per token. StepFun’s tech team adds the internals: StepFun ran its own evaluations at the High reasoning setting. Rivals in its chart ran at Max effort , so the comparison is not like-for-like. Results reported on the Hugging Face card : Independent numbers come from Artificial Analysis via OpenRouter . The model scores 43.7 on the Intelligence Index. It hits 88.3% on AA-LCR and 46.5% on Humanity’s Last Exam. GDPval-AA lands at 54.3%. Vals AI results show clear weak spots. SRE Bench is 0.4%. Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark is 9.2%. On finance, StepFun’s chart shows 66.4% on FrontierFinance . That beats GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3, but trails Claude Opus 5 at 69.7%. Benchmark rows come from StepFun’s comparison chart, as transcribed by CellCog and eesel . This is a data-center model. The FP8 checkpoint alone is 650.32 GB . Listed configurations : vLLM and SGLang ship dedicated Docker images with OpenAI-compatible APIs. On Blackwell, expert-parallel modes use the MegaMoE backend. StepFun recommends temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95 and top_k 0. The StepFun API charges $1.00 per 1M input tokens and $2.70 per 1M output tokens. Cache hits cost $0.10 per 1M. Output pricing includes reasoning tokens. The API supports low, medium and high reasoning effort, tool calling and JSON Schema output. item.title: DeepSeek Just Released V4.1-Flash-1017, Scores 77.0 on DeepSWE, Opens Search API
item.abstract: DeepSeek has just released DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 , a new checkpoint of its V4.1-Flash model. It is live on the DeepSeek website, app and API . DeepSeek claims stronger scores, faster task completion and shorter outputs than the September V4.1-Flash release . The company calls it a Pareto improvement in performance and cost. Alongside it, DeepSeek opened its Search and Fetch APIs to every developer. For agent builders, that means a cheaper coding model plus a first-party web layer behind one API key. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is an updated post-training checkpoint of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, served through the deepseek-flash model name. The architecture details below come from the V4.1-Flash technical report . DeepSeek team states that DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 uses reinforcement learning with self-feedback for end-to-end project work. Its examples run from game creation to 3D modeling. It is tuned for DeepSeek Harness , Tencent CodeBuddy and WorkBuddy. DeepSeek recommends DeepSeek Harness v0.2.1-rc.1 or later. V4.1-Flash is a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 40 Transformer layers. They split into a 20-layer causal encoder and a 20-layer decoder. All scores below are DeepSeek’s own figures . DeepSeek ran Terminal-Bench 4.0 in Claude Code and DeepSWE in Mini-SWE-V2. ZeroBench-main uses Pass@5. The 1017 checkpoint leads on DeepSWE, Automation-Bench, Agents’ Last Exam and Apex Bench. Claude Opus 5 still leads on Terminal-Bench 4.0, ProgramBench, NL2Repo and HLE. The Search API returns ranked web results for a query. The Fetch API returns a single page as Markdown. DeepSeek says its in-house engine serves hundreds of millions of requests daily. Call the model with deepseek-flash through OpenAI or Anthropic-format endpoints. Peak pricing is $0.30 per 1M cache-miss input tokens and $1.20 per 1M output tokens. Off-peak rates are half. item.title: 90% of US working hours are spent on tasks not covered well by AI benchmarks
item.abstract:
AI benchmarks have multiplied in recent years, but coverage of economically valuable work remains limited. To measure this, we compiled relevant benchmarks to measure their coverage of American jobs. This Benchmark Map is our first step toward building a comprehensive, continuously updated resource for understanding AI capabilities across the economy. Each tile represents one of the 923 O*NET occupations making up the US labor force, grouped into 22 job families. Occupations are shaded according to the share of their tasks which are represented in our initial list of AI benchmarks. A single benchmark prompt can be mapped to multiple O*NET tasks. In our data set: only 208 of 923 occupations have a task with at least 5 benchmark prompts , and 6 of 22 job families have no such occupations. Our findings suggest that 90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks . This makes it very hard to know how good AI models are at the work Americans actually do. The coverage of existing benchmarks is not random, either. Our map suggests that the AI community is focusing on the largest labor markets first: Adjusted probability of task coverage Annualized occupation wage bill (log scale) Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023) . Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level. For example, benchmarks in our initial list heavily cover AI-exposed lawyers’ tasks, but barely cover any of the O*NET tasks of similarly AI-exposed legal secretaries or court clerks. The long tail of smaller, middle-income knowledge work jobs appears undercovered. As we build out our coverage of model capabilities across the economy, we hope to both surface and help fill more gaps in our understanding of what models can do. To break down the economy into sectors, occupations, and tasks, we used the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy. O*NET divides the US workforce into 923 occupations; for each occupation, O*NET attempts to provide a comprehensive list of “tasks” which make up the occupation, totaling 18,797 tasks across all occupations. To measure benchmark coverage, we start with a list of 29 benchmarks selected for their quality and economic relevance. (The full list and selection criteria are in the Benchmark Index tab). In selecting benchmarks for this list, we prioritized: Following work by Wang et al. , we then ask an LLM judge to tag each benchmark prompt with as many O*NET tasks as it thinks correspond to that prompt. We validate our LLM tagging with human expert tags on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, a subset of this list of 29. On the Benchmark Map, an O*NET task counts as “covered” if our LLM judge has mapped it to at least 5 prompts from our 29 benchmarks. To estimate the total share of working hours Americans spend on tasks covered by benchmarks on this list, we combine our coverage estimates with Hatgis-Kessell et al. ’s LLM-derived estimates of the working time share of each O*NET task. A more detailed account of our methodology can be found in the Methodology tab. Our estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. This is not a complete or perfectly representative sample of the broader universe of unsaturated, public, agentic economic benchmarks. Any incomplete list will necessarily bias down estimates of economic coverage, and it is difficult to bound that bias. We want to stress, therefore, that these results are provisional. We will update them as we expand the initial benchmark list. We also capped the number of included benchmarks in each job family in order to maximize breadth of coverage. We think this makes our estimate of economy-wide benchmark coverage more accurate, at the cost of biasing down our estimates of coverage in the most-benchmarked job families (e.g. software engineering). By selecting for unsaturated benchmarks, we risk understating benchmark coverage on O*NET tasks which are easier for LLMs to complete. On the other hand, including saturated benchmarks would risk overstating benchmark coverage if saturation is downstream of lower task realism. The latter claim seems likely, given that benchmarks often overstate LLM performance in real-world deployments. We think that the bias from including saturated benchmarks would be greater than the bias from excluding them, but neither option is ideal. Finally, while we outline our benchmark selection criteria in the Benchmark Index tab, several criteria (like “Economic Realism”) are difficult to formalize and introduce some subjectivity in our choices. The benchmarks in our index have relatively deep and narrow coverage of the overall economy. They disproportionately focus on the economic tasks most exposed to AI automation (as measured by Eloundou et al. ), with O*NET tasks rated as “exposed” about 6x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than tasks rated “unexposed”. This makes sense: benchmarks are designed to measure AI progress, and AI progress is most plausible on the most AI-exposed tasks. This explains why benchmarks are full of tasks in Software Engineering and Financial Analysis while sparse on tasks in Truck Driving and Gas Plant Operation. But even after controlling for AI-exposure, O*NET tasks from occupations with larger wage bills are significantly overrepresented among benchmark prompts: Adjusted probability of task coverage Annualized occupation wage bill (log scale) Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023) . Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level. After controlling for occupation and AI-exposure score, O*NET “task importance” is another predictor of benchmark coverage. In particular, O*NET tasks come with domain expert estimates of the importance of the task for its occupation on a scale of 1-5. We find that the tasks scored most important are about 6–10x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than those scored least important: Adjusted probability of task coverage O*NET task importance (1–5 rating scale) Each point shows the estimated probability that, controlling for occupation, an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag and a given quintile O*NET importance score is covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023) . Importance quintiles are calculated from O*NET importance scores. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and importance quintiles, with occupation fixed effects. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.

item.title: Meta shakes up the frontiers, open and closed
item.abstract: This has been a week where the balance of American open-weight models took a step change back toward the frontier. Meta took the lead of this charge with Muse Spark Open , which is now the strongest American-made open model by quite some margin, but the addition of Reflection’s first model Beam is also relevant. Without these two models, there would be 20+ open-weight models built and released by Chinese companies better than the best Western models. At the time of writing this, Mistral has also announced a strong model, Mistral Large 4 , with an index score of 38 (see below), but its weights are not yet released. There are rumors of a few more strong American open-weight models coming from other organizations too! In many ways, the gap between the best American and Chinese models has been reduced roughly by half. We’ve gone from the best American open models being largely irrelevant to consumers who require the cutting edge of performance, to them being behind but relevant. This paints the picture of the cut-throat, competitive nature of the frontier model business. Reflection and Mistral announced their model scores and Meta dropped the weights of a smarter model before these other two labs could get their own weights out. All of these models are competing with Chinese models released months ago, where the industry is collectively asking — where have Kimi and Zhipu AI been since the releases of GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 on Aug. 18th and Jul. 16th, respectively? That is a very nuanced question, which I’ll dig into another time. Today’s piece is focused on Meta’s turnaround, what Muse Spark Open means for the ecosystem, and the balance of power across Western frontier labs. One thing we see again and again at Interconnects through our open model analysis is that Western open-weight models get astonishingly more adoption than Chinese models with the same performance-to-size footprint (even though the Chinese models usually come out first)! Muse Spark Open is landing into this environment, at the same time as when open-ended LLM agents are finally real (~ GLM 5.2 capabilities and on ). Riding off a rapid increase in performance of Chinese models, the open ecosystem has been living through an acceleration in demand. The inference providers are rapidly scaling, the open post-training economy is forming, and countless enterprises are looking to own their intelligence. Muse Spark Open’s performance falls somewhere above GLM 5.2, near DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and behind GLM 5.3 or Kimi K3. It should be squarely “good enough” to slot right into this. For some background, from the Muse Spark Open model card on Hugging Face: Muse Spark Open is an 816B total/42B active parameter open weights model with a context window of 1M tokens. Built for coding and agentic work, Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal. This open weights version has additional safety post-training to make it more robust against misuse as a standalone model without system guardrails. We recommend deploying Muse Spark Open as part of a broader AI system, with additional guardrails suited to the specific use case. Here’s the distribution of the various Muse models on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. This is included to loop back to the original model card snippet. It was shared that this open-weight model underwent additional safety training to prepare for this open release. Many observers saw this release as potentially a model that was “broken” during the safety training, as it came out after Muse Spark 1.3. In reality, this was much more likely a safety tune of Muse Spark 1.2, which would only be a 1 point drop on Artificial Analysis to shore up safety behaviors. When Meta released Muse Glimmer , the 30B agentic model, Alex Wang said that they were preparing to release the Muse Spark 1.2 model as open weights, which fits with the above. If anything will hold Muse Spark Open back, it’ll be the specific license they designed for it. In summary, this custom license has pretty much all of the restrictive license behaviors we’ve seen (and criticized here) in the last few years of building with open models. They are as follows: Users of the models in products must display “Built with Muse” on their products. Meta did this with Llama, and Kimi has tried it, but almost no one complies. There is a revenue-gating factor, where companies that make more than $20M per month across their entire business deploying the model need a separate license with Meta. Other prominent open model providers are doing this too, in order to set up revenue share agreements for re-selling inference. Muse Spark Open makes you agree to an acceptable use policy, which in the true “open source software” corner of the world makes this model extremely not open-source. All of the above applies to outputs from the model as well, and derivatives, so there is legal ambiguity if you can safely use the model for synthetic data. The license does permit using Muse Spark Open for internal research and applications. We’re at a weird equilibrium where this license is complex and unproven in court, but many players will likely ignore it. Many, many people will build on this model from various inference providers, and Meta will only likely go after egregious violations. For now, licenses haven’t been the determining factor of AI adoption, but this could change in the future. This is why we think it’s an unnecessary strategic risk for labs trying to compete and regain adoption to have complex, non-standard open licenses for their models. Just a few days before Muse Spark Open, Meta unveiled their closed frontier models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full . 1 On traditional benchmarks, these are very strong models only behind Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 and similar to OpenAI’s GPT-6-Astra or Google’s Gemini-4-Argon. These major releases are coming just over a year out from Meta’s massive AI redirection, characterized by CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s Personal Superintelligence post, which got a lot of criticism at the time. Meta is the only American company with frontier open and closed models. Alibaba’s Qwen has followed a similar strategy, but with a far more open-leaning approach. The vibe checks across all of these models have been solid, but the expectations were for them to not immediately challenge the level of refinement of the most recent Anthropic and OpenAI models in real-world usage. I’m excited to try them more — time to sign up for another AI subscription. I like this recent run of form from Meta, driving their own products and directions in the popular Muse agent, taking wins like the leading US open-weight crown when useful. Whether or not it’s financially successful, it’s a unique perspective that fits their history as a business. It often feels like there’s a revolving door of which lab is nipping at the heels of the Anthropic-OpenAI leading duo. It’s not clear that in the long run Gemini and xAI are out of it, but those two are much more muddled in their offerings than Meta today. If you listen to Zuck and Alexandr Wang on The Cheeky Pint , they clearly had a very specific vision of a high-ownership, high-compute per researcher lab that I would expect to pay off. Many labs die due to layers of bureaucracy and misaligned incentives. Meanwhile Alex Wang has over 200 direct reports — i.e. it’s a very flat org with minimal management — and they’re releasing very consistent model and product improvements. Much of my worldview of building models is that you need the resources, the compute, the data, and the talent (all downstream of large sums of money), but organizing them is very hard. Gemini is sometimes described as a place where it’s impossible to get any work done or grow — which is embellishing the issue, as many people love it there, but there are kernels of truth to it. Layers of management easily get in the way of making a great model.

item.title: Building trust in AI agents: A production-ready evaluation framework with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.abstract: Every organization racing to deploy AI agents faces the same reckoning: an agent that demos beautifully can quietly degrade in production, and by the time a human notices, the trust is already broken. Where traditional software fails loudly, agents fail softly. They return an answer that looks confident, reads fluently, and is wrong. When that answer drives a real business decision, the cost is not a broken feature. It’s a broken relationship with the user. That’s the quality problem at its core. The challenge is therefore not building agents that work once, but proving they keep working, at scale, across every sub-agent, every workflow, and every release. The teams that win the agent era will be the ones who treat quality not as a final QA step but as the operating system of the agent itself: continuously measured, automatically defended, and improved with every interaction. In this post, we show how we built a continuous quality loop for production-ready agentic solutions at scale using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The solution uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and other AWS services for internal use, so sellers and sales leaders can ask business questions in plain English from Amazon Quick. Behind that single experience, several specialized sub-agents work together: the Performance Insights Agent for territory-scoped revenue and performance, the Customer Insights Agent for customer intelligence, the Data Insights Agent for text-to-SQL over foundational datasets, and direct dashboard access. Answers are scoped to each user’s territory and role-level security. Field teams use these answers to assist in planning account strategy, prepare for customer meetings, so the numbers must be right. The most damaging failure is not a crash. It’s a fluent, confident answer that is quietly wrong. Before launch, when we evaluated the Customer Insights Agent, we found exactly that: Through the different runs, monitoring stayed green. It told us the system had responded, not whether the answer was right. Had these errors shipped uncaught, the field would have paid for them. A seller who repeats an inflated figure can lose credibility with the customer. This is exactly why we caught it before launch. The risk doesn’t end at launch: it grows with every new agent and every change to data, prompts, code, or models. It also grows without any release, because upstream pipelines refresh the data every week. Coordinated releases introduce a related risk: when a data change, a tool change, and a paired prompt update are meant to ship together but land apart, the system runs mismatched until all changes catch up. In one pre-production test, that mismatch window by itself dropped the pass rate from 78 percent to 38 percent. To catch failures like these, before every release and continuously in production, we need a framework that can show whether answers are grounded and correct, and trace each failure back to its root cause in the data, the prompt, or the agent’s code. At AWS, the Sales, Marketing, and Global Services (SMGS) Operations team developed a production multi-agent system serving AWS Field Sales worldwide. It serves two distinct audiences. For field sales teams, it replaces hours of manual data analysis with on-demand, conversational intelligence, helping sellers understand the health of their business, surface risks and opportunities, and take action faster. For leadership, it powers business management cadences including Weekly Business Reviews (WBRs), surfacing the signals that matter across the portfolio without requiring manual report preparation. The same agentic system serves both the seller on the front line and the leader reviewing performance at scale. The agentic system orchestrates a growing portfolio of specialized sub-agents, each owning a distinct capability domain. Among them: the Performance Insights Agent generates natural-language business intelligence narratives from complex sales data, turning raw metrics into actionable seller insights. The Customer Insights Agent assembles a 360-degree view of each customer by synthesizing signals across product usage, support history, contract status, and engagement data, helping sellers understand where a customer is in their journey and what they need next. The Data Insights Agent is a text-to-SQL agent that account teams use to query structured analytics data in plain English without writing a single line of SQL. These three agents are the ones referenced throughout the rest of this post. Coordinating these agents reliably at scale made one thing clear: agentic quality wasn’t an operational concern to manage later. It was the prerequisite for operating. A single degraded sub-agent can silently corrupt every response downstream, and traditional monitoring won’t catch it. That reality made a full lifecycle evaluation framework not optional but necessary. AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is the connective tissue powering it, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (safety), Amazon CloudWatch (metrics, alarms, tracing), Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and Amazon Redshift (evaluation persistence), Amazon Quick (dashboards), and AWS Lambda (custom evaluators). In this post, we share how we tackled the hardest operational challenges in running AI agents at enterprise scale, and how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations became the backbone of agent quality. Specifically, we cover: Traditional software is deterministic: the same input produces the same output. Machine learning (ML) models introduced probabilistic outputs, and MLOps emerged to manage their training, versioning, monitoring, and re-training. AI agents add a third layer of operational complexity: autonomous, multi-step reasoning, where the question shifts from “did something break?” to “is the agent making sound decisions across its entire reasoning chain?” Agents inherit the hard problems of both predecessors, and introduce some new ones. They’re non-deterministic, following different reasoning paths for identical inputs. They make cascading decisions across routing, tool selection, and synthesis, where a single step can fail quietly and corrupt everything downstream. Most critically, they degrade silently: latency stays low, error rates stay flat, yet the quality of agent response erodes, because the agent is still responding . It is just responding wrong . Agent evaluation is the practice of catching exactly that. It spans five dimensions: safety (is it behaving within defined boundaries?), quality (is the agent producing correct, coherent, grounded responses?), performance (is it fast and reliable enough?), cost (is it running efficiently at scale?), and operational control (can we detect, diagnose, and remediate issues quickly?). A mature evaluation practice addresses five continuously, throughout the full agent lifecycle. In this post, we share how we operationalize five evaluation dimensions across a production multi-agent system. Safety and security is our first priority. No agent ships, and no agent keeps running, if it can’t meet its safety bar. Quality gets the most space in this post because it’s the hardest of the five to get right and benefits most from a dedicated framework, but it doesn’t outrank safety. Performance, cost, and operational control are woven into every stage of the lifecycle alongside both. Critically, this framework applies at every level of the agent hierarchy. At the tool level , each capability (a customer disambiguation tool, graph retrieval tool) has its own evaluation contract. At the agent level , each sub-agent is evaluated end-to-end. At the multi-agent level , orchestration paths are evaluated for coherence, correct routing, and synthesis accuracy across agent boundaries. The nine stages apply at three levels simultaneously, and this hierarchy is not specific to this product. It’s the right mental model when we build or integrate new production agents.

item.title: 20 Jev Alternatives: The Decision Models Taking On TypeSafe in 2026
item.abstract: TypeSafe launched Jev on September 15, 2026. It is a decision model, not a chatbot. You define the allowed answers, and Jev returns a label, a score or a yes/no probability. In about 4 weeks, at least 20 Jev alternatives shipped. They come from Cloudflare, OpenAI, Perplexity, Liquid AI, AWS’s Strands Labs and independent developers. This guide compares each one on size, license, hardware, pricing, Jev API compatibility and published benchmarks. Jev is TypeSafe’s first ‘System One’ model. You send a state, such as a ticket or log line. You also send typed questions: Choice, Score or Noul (yes/no). Jev scores every question in one parallel pass and generates no text. TypeSafe’s docs list $0.042 per 1M input tokens, with free output. Context is 64k tokens per request. Input is text only. Weights are closed, and access runs through a waitlist. TypeSafe’s workflow evals put Jev at 67.8% agreement and 0.4 s per case. That leaves 4 gaps developers keep raising: no images, no self-hosting, no published size and no fine-tuning. The 20 models below fill some or all of them. Most figures below are self-reported. The suites differ: JevBench, Decision Index, typed-decisions and Respan’s behavior benchmark. Scores across suites are not comparable. The one multi-model third-party table comes from Respan , which sells a competing model. Cloudflare announced Clef on October 1, 2026. Clef is 27B on Qwen3.8-27B with a vision encoder. Clef-flash is 9B on Qwen3.5-9B. Both are Apache-2.0 on Hugging Face and served on Workers AI. They accept text, JSON and up to 4 images per request. Workers AI pricing is $0.24 (Clef) and $0.038 (Clef-flash) per 1M input tokens. Cloudflare calls the API fully Jev-compatible. In its own run, Clef scored 94.20 BANKING77 F1 versus Jev’s 79.74. Jev still wins GPQA Diamond, 78.3 versus 48.0. Liquid AI’s d1 family has hosted d1 and d1-ultra, plus 2 open models. d1-3B (3.1B) runs on LFM2.5-VL-3B. d1-omni-600M (587M) adds audio clips up to 30 s. The open weights use the LFM Open License. Liquid’s guide calls d1 through TypeSafe’s own SDK with a different base URL. Liquid reports d1-3B at 48.57 on Decision Index 0.2.1. It also reports 8 ms latency on an RTX 4090. Hosted parameter counts and paid rates are not disclosed. OpenAI released the Decisions API in public beta on October 6, 2026. It runs only on gpt-6-luna. It accepts text plus base64 images. Question types are predicate, choice and score. Pricing is $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with output not billed. The schema is OpenAI’s own, so it is not Jev-compatible. OpenAI claims about 10x faster responses than the Responses API. No benchmarks are published. Perplexity’s pplx-decider-v1-27b is a Qwen3.8-27B fine-tune under Apache-2.0. It reads text, JSON and up to 8 images per question. The API allows 128 questions and 255 options per request. The current pricing is $0.02 per 1M input tokens for v1.2 (27B). A 4B flash-v1.2 costs $0.01. On Perplexity’s 11-task panel, it scored 85.71% versus Jev’s 84.51%. Jev still won BBH, 94.27 versus 82.80. meraGPT announced Decider 1 on September 22, 2026. It is a hosted, closed-weight, text-only model. It allows up to 10 Choice labels and a 4,096-token context. The model page lists $0.04 per 1M input tokens. It exposes /v1/systemone and works with the TypeSafe SDK. On meraGPT’s typed-decisions run, it scored 0.768 versus Jev’s 0.727. An independent review notes its ECE of 0.180 trails Jev’s 0.144. Span-01 is a behavior-scoring model, not a general decision model. It returns present, absent or not_observable probabilities. It costs $0.02 per 1M input tokens. Span-01 Lite is free. Respan claims 0.843 overall F1 on its Behavior Benchmark. Its own blog table shows a lower 0.806, with GPT-6 Sol ahead at 0.885. Size, base model and license are not disclosed. Standard One ships as 3B and 8B models, both open and hosted. The 8B is a LoRA on Ministral-3-8B under Apache-2.0. It reads text and images, with a 32,768-token context. It serves /v1/systemone. Hosted text pricing is $0.018 (3B) and $0.035 (8B) per 1M tokens. On JevBench public hard, the 8B scored 54.95% versus Jev’s 72.07%. It led on realistic transfer, 90.83% versus 86.67%. Both runs are publisher-measured. Together trained Tev1 as a LoRA SFT of Qwen3.5-4B. It cost about $17 and 25 minutes on 37,840 examples. It picks from 2 to 24 options. The model card says the weights license is still being finalized. It answers through chat completions, not a native Jev endpoint. Respan measured 0.901 accuracy and 0.031 ECE, the best ECE in its table. Together warns its logprobs are not calibrated confidence. Fastino’s GLiNER2.5-Decide is a 340M DeBERTa-v3-large encoder under Apache 2.0. It handles decisions, span extraction and relations in one pass. A 1B and a 287M multilingual variant also exist. On Fastino’s 17-domain set, the model card lists 60.2% exact match. p50 latency is 167.3 ms on a 48-vCPU Xeon. It is not Jev API-compatible. AWS’s Strands Labs introduced Strands Decider on October 1, 2026. It is about 1.9B: Qwen3.5-2B-Base plus a pointer head. The repo publishes 246,678 training rows and the full recipe. One RTX 3090 trains it in about 11 hours. It serves a local /v1/systemone endpoint under Apache-2.0. The v1 checkpoint scored 180 of 231 (77.9%) on JevBench public. Median latency is 115 ms on an RTX 3090. Kev comes in 0.8B, 4B, 9B and 27B sizes on Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8. Kev-4B is a LoRA plus pointer head under Apache-2.0. It supports 255 options. The TypeSafe SDK works against it unchanged. Kev-4B fits a 24 GB GPU or a 32 GB Apple Silicon Mac. Respan measured 0.833 accuracy and a 0.060 flip rate. Self-reported MMLU-Pro is 0.565 versus Jev’s 0.840. Option order can change its answers. Mapika’s Decider ships 0.8B to 35B-A3B variants on Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4. A decider-2b-vision model adds images. Everything is Apache-2.0, with 32k context and /v1/systemone. On the JevBench public hard tier, decider-12b v1 tied Jev at 0.730. The 4B GGUF Q4_K_M is 2.7 GB and runs on CPU. The 4B’s ECE is 0.184 on hard items, so expect overconfidence. Bespoke-Nimble-9B is a 165 MiB LoRA on Qwen3.5-9B, Apache-2.0 on Hugging Face. The current card lists 255 choices and 8,192 tokens. It reads English text only. On Bespoke’s 324-example held-out set, Nimble scored 90.12% versus Jev’s 93.21%. Latency is about 106 ms on an H100. It trained on only 2,676 examples, and its probabilities are not calibrated. Laya is a ModernBERT-based family with 421M English and 322M multilingual checkpoints. It is Apache-2.0 and text only. The laya-serve server exposes a Jev-shaped /v1/systemone endpoint. The typed-decisions checkpoint scored 0.766 versus Jev’s 0.727. On Banking77, it scored 0.425 versus 0.870. Respan measured 0.542 accuracy and a 0.396 injection success rate. p50 latency is 32.8 ms on a T4. Von is a 395M ModernBERT-large encoder with an option-marker head. It scores all options in one bidirectional pass. It is Apache-2.0 with an 8,192-token context. The repo reports 0.096 s p50 on 4 vCPUs and 0.023 s on an A10G. Respan measured Von 1.2 at 0.422 accuracy, the lowest in its table. Its calibration is tuned to JevBench and can mislead out of domain. Open-Jev ships 2B, 9B and 27B adapters on Qwen3.5 bases. Open-Jev-9B adds a scalar head and fits one 16 GB GPU. It matches the /v1/systemone request shape but claims no parity. On a 231-task JevBench subset, the project reports 77.49% for 9B and 85.28% for 27B v1.1. Each candidate is capped at 4,096 tokens. Numeric and timeline tasks are weak. This OpenJev reads decisions from NVIDIA’s DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B (4B active). It accepts text plus up to 8 images. It uses the same wire API, so Jev SDKs work unchanged. The project reports 87.4% on JevBench public and 30 ms p50 at 49 tokens. A free hosted endpoint gives 100M tokens per account. Self-hosting needs an NVIDIA GPU with at least 24 GB. InnerJev comes from a Fudan, Tongji and King’s College London team.

item.title: 霸榜三大基準！優必選 Thinker-WM：多模態統一表徵，單模型實現六大能力
item.abstract: 霸榜三大基準！優必選 Thinker-WM：多模態統一表徵，單模型實現六大能力 量子位的朋友們 2026-10-16 16:00:31 來源： 量子位 優必選 Thinker-WM在三大公認具身世界模型基準評測中全部拿下第一名 01 三大基準全榜登頂，Thinker-WM 斬獲三項第一 日前，優必選 Thinker-WM在三大公認具身世界模型基準評測中全部拿下第一名，重新整理行業成績： WorldOlympiad ： Thinker‑WM 取得綜合得分 0.740 位列榜首。該基準基於大量真實機器人互動資料構建，覆蓋十餘種不同機器人本體與多類相機配置，重點考核模型跨機器人形態、跨視角的泛化能力。模型取得 3D 一致性 0.531、互動保真度 0.765，兩項單項指標位居全部參評模型首位，體現模型對三維幾何結構與機器人互動過程的精準建模能力。 EWMBench： Thinker‑WM 取得綜合總分 4.66，超過 Qwen‑RobotWorld、Sora2 等主流模型。EWMBench 完整考核場景一致性、機器人末端運動正確性、指令語義對齊三大能力維度。得益於表徵層面的多模態聯合建模，Thinker‑WM 在反映機器人軌跡時空匹配的 nDTW（歸一化動態時間規整）、表徵運動速度與加速度合理性的 Dyn（動力學一致性）等機器人運動核心指標上實現領先。 WorldArena1.0 Track-1： 在模擬環境基準 WorldArena Track‑1，Thinker‑WM 在視覺畫質、內容一致性、物理合理性、3D 幾何精度、指令遵循等 12 項關鍵評價維度整體領先，兼顧模擬環境下視覺生成質量與物理互動可信度。Thinker‑WM 以表徵層統一的 Unified Dynamic Transformer（UDT）為核心，將 RGB 影像、度量深度、機器人動作納入同一套共享動態表徵聯合演化，實現影片‑動作聯合生成、世界預測、策略推理、影片轉動作、逆動力學等多項能力合一，為具身智慧提供新一代基礎世界模型底座。 02 Thinker-WM技術突破：表徵層面實現視覺、幾何、動作多模態統一 讓機器人在真實世界落地幹活，最難的不是識別眼前物體，而是預判環境下一步變化。這也是世界模型存在的價值與意義，而過往世界模型普遍採用 “拼接式” 方案：影片生成負責畫面、策略網路負責動作、幾何預測負責空間資訊，模組獨立計算，再通過介面拼接輸出。 但這套技術模型的問題在於，動作改變環境、環境約束動作，幾何結構同時影響兩者，物理上緊密耦合的訊號被拆分到不同模組，丟失其內在因果關聯。 舉個例子，“一個杯子被推下桌子”這件事情，在語言裡是一句話描述，在動作裡是一串關節命令，在影片裡是一段穿越畫面的物體運動，在深度裡是一組連續變化的距離場。四種表述指向的是同一個事件，而不是四個不同的物件。所以，要求模型生成其中任何一種，本質上都是在追問同一個過程。 但這種重疊又是不完全的。動作既不攜帶外觀，也不攜帶上下文，同樣的關節命令，放在空桌子上和放在雜亂的桌子上，含義完全不同。語言也不攜帶時空細節，“杯子被推下桌子”這句話，既沒有規定從哪一側推、用多大力、以什麼速度推，也沒有規定手的具體軌跡、杯子翻轉幾圈、最終落在哪裡。影片不攜帶顯式幾何和度量，其僅使用一系列畫素表示，既不知道杯子的尺寸，也不知道杯子的距離。深度也不攜帶外觀、命名語義和意圖，它給出表面在哪裡、如何遮擋、如何接觸，卻不告訴你那是杯子還是桌布，更不告訴你為什麼要推它。 針對這個問題，優必選 Thinker 團隊給出全新解法：不在介面處做簡單合併，而是在表徵層面實現多模態統一。Thinker-WM（Thinker World Model）作為優必選自研統一多模態世界模型，將 RGB 影片、深度和機器人動作編碼至同一個中間表徵空間，依靠一組共享參數聯合演化。外觀、幾何、動作不再是三條獨立流水線，而是同一個世界演化過程的三種表達形態。也就是說，Thinker-WM 的底層設計邏輯可以概括為：不同模態是同一過程的不同表述；模型將它們對齊到共享表徵空間，並在這一共享表徵上進行推理，而不是在模態介面上做條件組合。 Thinker-WM：視覺、幾何與動作的統一建模框架 具體來看，RGB影像、深度資訊、機器人動作分別通過各自的編碼器對映到統一潛在空間，送入共享的統一動態Transformer（Unified Dynamics Transformer, UDT）進行聯合時序建模，最終由各自的解碼器還原輸出影片、深度圖、機器人可執行動作。這就意味著多模態的交互發生在Transformer內部，視覺token、幾何token和動作token通過同一個注意力機制直接交換資訊，而不是在輸入或輸出層做淺層拼接。 幾何資訊也不再只是輔助監督訊號。Thinker-WM 把深度作為原生生成模態，與影片共享一致的潛在拓撲和時空組織。深度監督直接塑造共享表徵，讓物理空間結構成為世界模型的 “母語”，而非後期外掛補充模組，從而也能幫助人形機器人更準確地理解物理空間。統一建模的價值，也體現在機器人的實際執行效果上。在 RoboTwin 單任務消融實驗中，引入深度模態後，操作成功率較無深度基線提升了 15 個百分點 ，說明空間幾何資訊不僅有助於模型理解場景，也能改善動作生成與任務執行。 03 3萬小時異構資料，讓一個模型，解鎖六種能力 依託多模態統一表徵，所有模態共享同一組參數，Thinker-WM 可以通過靈活切換條件模態與生成模態，支援六大能力模式。 同一份權重，既能預判、想像未來畫面，也能反向推演機器人執行軌跡，還能從影片中提取動作資訊，這正是統一表徵帶來的核心技術紅利。 04 3萬小時異構資料，撐起通用世界模型底座 統一表徵能力的背後，是優必選規模豐富、型別多元的訓練資料支撐。Thinker-WM 訓練語料在具身智慧領域具備可觀體量： 約2萬小時第一人稱人類影片 ：覆蓋家庭、商業零售、工業等場景，補足機器人遙操作難以低成本獲取的任務、物體與場景多樣性，同時配套約 1 千小時的對齊深度資料。 約1萬小時真實機器人資料 ：來自多款不同形態機器人，提供視覺觀測與可執行動作的配對監督，其中約 3 千小時配套對齊深度標註。 約1千小時模擬資料 ：提供高精度幾何、物理監督訊號。 不同機器人動作空間、座標系、控制協議差異巨大。Thinker-WM 的統一思想不僅應用於模型框架上，也應用於資料選擇中。該模型統一使用末端位姿表示所有機器人動作，同時為不同機器人在token中嵌入專屬標籤。這樣不同形態的機器人可以共享同一個生成空間，又能夠保留精準的本體控制能力。 05 資料 Infra：讓海量異構資料高效支撐統一模型訓練 海量資料要轉化為模型能力，離不開穩定、高效的資料基礎設施。面對不同機器人、人類影片與模擬資料在格式、模態和標註上的差異，優必選 Thinker 團隊構建了 Data Factory，將資料管理與訓練取樣解耦，讓多源資料按模型需求靈活組合。 Data Factory：從多源異構資料到統一模型訓練 Data Factory 圍繞三個關鍵環節支撐訓練： 統一組織 影片、狀態、動作與語言資訊，按需生成不同訓練模式所需的樣本；通過 分層質檢 過濾異常片段，檢查深度與影片對齊，確保訓練訊號可靠；通過 非同步預取與編碼複用 提前準備訓練資料，減少等待與重複計算。 這套資料基礎設施，讓多源異構資料能夠被可靠組織、靈活呼叫、高效供給，為 Thinker-WM 六種能力模式的聯合訓練與持續迭代提供工程支撐。 06 通過Motion Probe實驗設計，輕量化實驗：驗證跨模態表徵真實耦合 表徵層面統一多模態，聽起來是架構設計上的創新，但有一個核心疑問：模型究竟是真的在共享空間學到視覺、幾何、動作之間的耦合關聯，還是隻是並行處理多路資訊，把不同模態簡單放在一起？ 為回答這個問題，優必選Thinker 團隊設計了輕量級 Motion Probe（運動探針）驗證實驗。研究團隊在凍結的UDT視覺表徵上接一個極小的運動預測頭，只訓練這個頭，看能否從純視覺表徵中恢復出末端執行器的位移。 Motion Probe示意圖 實驗結果證實猜想：探針預測誤差很低。即使沒有動作監督，視覺表徵中也已經編碼了與動作相關的運動資訊。這一結果直接證明，表徵層面的多模態統一真實生效，視覺感知和動作規劃不是兩條相互獨立的鏈路，而是在共享潛在空間裡實現深度耦合。 07 這意味著什麼 這也進一步說明，Thinker-WM本次技術的突破的，價值遠不止一次刷榜成果。它指明具身世界模型的底層新範式： 具身智慧的世界模型不應該是 “影片生成器 + 策略頭” 的簡單組合，而是一套完整統一的生成過程——視覺觀測、空間結構、動作規劃，是同一個物理世界過程的不同表達。 當機器人能夠在同一表徵空間內同步推演畫面變化、空間結構、動作軌跡，它對物理世界因果邏輯的理解便向前邁進一大步。這也是機器人從“可以執行任務幹活”，邁向“能夠理解真實世界”的關鍵躍遷。 Thinker-WM 現已完成在優必選機器人平臺上部署驗證，相關技術將持續賦能下一代具身智慧系統。 Thinker-WM 的探索不止本次成果釋出。模型技術報告與後續迭代版本將在優必選官方具身智慧開發者社群Thinker Cosmos 持續更新；世界模型二次開發能力開放計劃、技術解讀直播預告，也將第一時間面向開發者公佈。歡迎加入Thinker item.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
item.abstract: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I’ve sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner. I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here’s what that looks like: I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing: Start dev server and open in browser This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress. Then I clicked the “Start new voice chat” button—that’s not the microphone button, it’s the one to the right of it—and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked. I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it’s a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources. Here’s an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex: Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it’s not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don’t want it on the tag pages. I don’t want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they’re... published, like once they’re made public a month after they’ve gone out, I want them to show up on my search results. Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist . We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code. We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice: It was almost ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I’d have to sit at the keyboard for a while. Once I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request. I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead. You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR . I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR. You can see the end result at the new newsletters index page , or view the page for a previous monthly newsletter . The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages. GPT-6 Astra designed the page, and then tweaked that design based on my vocal feedback from glancing at the local preview across the kitchen. OpenAI love using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay —and they do work well in that environment. I don’t think this is going to be a daily driver for me though. I’ve written before about how much “work” I get done using ChatGPT voice mode on my phone while walking the dog—mostly research and brainstorming, but occasionally actual development work by having ChatGPT write and test out snippets of code. This feels different. The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn’t work vocally, makes this a much more powerful way of interacting with a coding agent. I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though. Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words. I mainly work from home, which is good because there’s no way I’d want to talk to my computer like this in a shared workspace! The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead. This is A new feature for my blog, built using my voice by Simon Willison, posted on 9th October 2026 . item.title: Websites are closing their doors to AI agents
item.abstract: AI Report Tech Websites are closing their doors to AI agents OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen. OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen. by Emma Roth Oct 17, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. But what happens when the rest of the internet won’t play nice? In recent weeks, users of services like Meta’s Muse, xAI’s Grok, OpenAI’s Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites. Yelp told TechCrunch that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets on behalf of users. JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have also confirmed that they’re blocking AI agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns. Some users say sites that previously worked with their AI agent are no longer accessible, including Cars.com and Amtrak , suggesting other companies could be quietly blocking them. Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and sued the AI startup , raising legal and practical questions about the future of agents on the web. At the time, Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its AI agents to shop on its website, adding that third-party companies that purchase items on behalf of customers “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate.” Perplexity responded by pointing out that Amazon doesn’t want AI agents roaming its platform because it won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads — which is an actual issue for the ecommerce giant. The AI startup likened its AI agent to an extension of the user, arguing that Amazon “does not believe in your right to hire labor, to have an assistant or an employee acting on your behalf.” While a judge later ordered Perplexity to stop its AI agents from shopping on its website, an appeals court overturned this ruling in August . Amazon has since filed an amended complaint . Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems This ongoing legal battle didn’t stop OpenAI, Meta, and Google from rolling out agents of their own. But they’re dealing with the same problems as Perplexity. Muse, Meta’s deceptively cute AI assistant, most recently faced the wrath of Amazon , which said its “continued access” violates its site policies. There are reports of xAI’s Grok , Instinct’s AI agent, and OpenAI’s Dots being unable to use Amazon as well. xAI owner Elon Musk responded by saying that maybe he “should start a competitor to Amazon.” The more places bots struggle to access, the greater the questions about how useful they are. “Does this impact the perceived value of the Anthropics and the OpenAIs? I would say absolutely,” Chris Canal, the CEO of the AI safety evaluator EquiStamp, tells The Verge . “One of the claims is that they’re going to permeate every aspect of our lives and be able to do anything that we could do online. If there are companies that are actively working to make that not happen, there are just fewer useful things the agents can do.” Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a post earlier this month . “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” the company says. “We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer.” Instead of trying to fight Amazon, the company has partnered with retailers like Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy, and others, allowing Muse to shop on their sites. At the same time, Shopify has also opened its network of storefronts to AI agents. The Verge reached out to OpenAI and Google with requests for comments on the roadblocks their AI agents are facing but didn’t immediately hear back. Instinct declined to comment. Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems, which have become ubiquitous across the web. Reports on Reddit suggest that Google is blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity,” while others have reported issues checking out on Walmart despite its Meta partnership. “There are all kinds of things that are set up not even to block agents, but to block in general bots or programs that are trying to scam or hack,” Canal adds. “These AI agents trigger those same safeguards.” The web architecture provider Cloudflare has also played a role in helping sites clamp down on unwanted AI visitors. After introducing a one-click block for AI crawlers in 2025, Cloudflare began blocking crawlers that simultaneously scrape websites for both search indexing and AI training. The move is part of Cloudflare’s efforts to save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is putting a strain on internet infrastructure and wreaking havoc on email inboxes, and which could eventually make it even harder than it already is to compete against bots when purchasing concert tickets, booking reservations, or trying to get ahold of certain products. While these blocks may help keep some AI agents and bots out of a website, Canal says they will ultimately make the web more “annoying” to use as more sites roll out interfaces to confirm you’re not a robot. “We could see them on a simple grocery shopping website soon, where you’re having to jump through a bunch of hoops to prove that you’re a human using the computer or your phone.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. item.title: [AINews] High Taste Testers Ep. 1
item.abstract: We are piloting a new show on Latent Space: High Taste Testers, a variant of our food show where we pull you in to a typical lunch conversation in San Francisco. All your favorite talking points, starting with Dev Day and going into the latest models and assistants, are here: AI News for 10/15/2026-10/16/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! US Open-Weights Push: Muse Spark Open and Reflection Beam Muse Spark Open (Meta) : An 816B-total, 42B-active MoE with open weights. Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index, the highest for a US open-weights model and 13 points above NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL at 26 ( AA ). Architecture and footprint : 62 layers, GQA with 16 KV heads, 8 of 256 experts active per token, a 1.8B Perception Encoder and 1M context. Inputs are text, image, video and audio; output is text. BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. Meta’s NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts, cutting weights to about 530GB. Meta says that fits on 4 Blackwell Ultra GPUs, 8 H200s or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Pricing and efficiency : Together, Fireworks and Baseten charge $1.25/$4.25 per M input/output tokens, with $0.15 cached input. AA puts the cost at $0.84 per index task, versus $2.01 for GLM-5.3 and $0.27 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. It uses 40k output tokens per task, the fewest among the top nine open models ( cost ). Vals counts 55.5M output tokens across its index, the fewest of any open model, but says input tokens drive most of its cost ( Vals ). Weak spot : It ranks last among the top nine open models on AA’s four agentic evals while leading open models on AA-Omniscience. Vals places it #12 among open-weight models and #38 overall ( Vals ). Arena ranks it the top US open model on Code Arena WebDev with 1511 points, #13 among open models ( Arena ). License : The custom Muse Model License requires “Built with Muse Spark Open” attribution. Model-as-a-Service businesses with more than $20M in annual revenue need a separate agreement with Meta. Ecosystem : mlx-lm had day-0 support with vision, plus an Apple blog post on RDMA-distributed inference across Mac Studios ( @zcbenz ). vLLM served RL rollouts during Muse training and supports the release at launch ( vLLM ). SemiAnalysis has added B200 configurations to InferenceX ( SemiAnalysis ). Criticism (opinion) : @teortaxesTex calls it “DOA” against the smaller, MIT-licensed V4.1 Flash. He also speculates, without evidence, that Meta withheld Spark 1.3 because of distillation from OpenAI ( speculation ). @alexandr_wang describes MSL as having built “a machine that builds new models.” Reflection Beam 1.0 : A 501B-total, 23B-active MoE with 1M context, released under Apache 2.0. The release includes BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 weights, a DFlash2 drafter, the open Mirror CLI harness Beam was trained on, and a safety report ( Reflection , safety report , Mirror ). Independent evals : AA scores it 30, #2 among US open models, using about 26k tokens per task. It reaches 48.5% on AutomationBench-AA but only 3.0% on Terminal-Bench 4.0. On AA-Omniscience it answers 33% correctly but hallucinates at 47% ( AA ). Arena places it #12 among open models in Agent Arena (±3.84%) and makes it the only non-Chinese model in the top 25 open models on Code WebDev ( Arena ). Architecture : Sliding-window attention with a 512 window in a 5:1 pattern, no RoPE, Llama-4-style global attention scaling, gated attention, QK-norm, sandwich norm, logit softcapping and no shared experts ( @eliebakouch ). Serving and RL : vLLM had day-0 support. On 4× B300 with NVFP4 at TP4, it measured 1,769 output tok/s at concurrency 16. SkyRL offers day-0 LoRA, full fine-tuning and MXFP8 RL, and reports +62% LoRA decode throughput (276→447 tok/s/GPU), which is a decode result, not an end-to-end training speedup ( vLLM , SkyRL ). Ollama is serving it free for a limited time, US-hosted with zero data retention ( Ollama ). Other open releases : StepFun released Step 5 Preview open weights ( Together ). Tencent shipped Hy Memory 2.0 and claims Hy-Memory-30B-A3B beats Opus 5 on memory frameworks ( Tencent ). Datalab released Indra, a 1M-parameter OCR model it says runs 15× faster than Tesseract on CPU ( @VikParuchuri ). Frontier Model Rollouts and the Decision-Model Category Gemini 4 Argon : Now available to Pro subscribers and in AI Studio Build ( @_philschmid , AI Studio ). Specs and pricing : The wide release raises the output limit to 1M tokens from 64K, sharing the window with input. Intro pricing is $2/$10 until Nov 30 ( DeepLearning.AI ). Results : Perplexity reports a new SOTA on its WANDR research benchmark ( @AravSrinivas ). Argon ranks #5 in Agent Arena at +13.2% ( Arena ). @MParakhin gives early praise for its math, with the caveat that it needs higher reasoning effort. Anthropic speed and price moves : Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10/$0.50 for prompts up to 100K tokens, about 90% cheaper than Haiku 4.5. It scores 39.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at max effort, versus 16.4% for GPT-6 Luna ( DL Weekly ). An Opus 5.5 fast mode at 2.5× speed is reported ( @kimmonismus ). Claude Code now gzips the conversation payload on every turn to cut latency ( ClaudeDevs ). OpenAI product updates : GPT-6 Astra Pro in ChatGPT now runs multiple agents on parts of a task in parallel, with faster responses and better tool use ( OpenAI ). GPT Live 1.1 improves multilingual voice, and nine new presets were recorded with native-speaking actors ( @reach_vb , OpenAIDevs ). Codex is believed to have one or two new models coming; this is unconfirmed speculation ( @kimmonismus ). Elorian Glimpse : A visual-thinking VLM that runs recurrent computation over latent visual states instead of text-only chain of thought. Claimed results : Elorian says it matches or beats Astra on 5 of 12 benchmarks at 17× lower token prices, trained on “hundreds of GPUs” ( @dustinvtran ). Informal test : @omarsar0 found 8 of 10 game boards fully correct, versus 5 of 10 for Gemini 3.8 Flash. Decision models (calibrated one-pass classifiers) : Liquid d1-ultra : Tops AA’s Decision Index at 65, ahead of Jev 1.14 at 57. Its non-hallucination rate rises to 85% from 2% for d1, but accuracy falls to 32% from 41%. Time per task is 92ms and price is $0.042 per M input tokens, with output free ( AA ). Perplexity pplx-decider v1.2 : Open weights in a 27B model at 2¢/M and a 4B Flash model at 1¢/M. The update adds reranking, single-pass multi-question inference that is up to 5× faster, and -latest slugs ( @AravSrinivas , @denisyarats ). Usage : OpenAI’s Live API added a Decisions API for fast tool delegation ( @juberti ). In one experiment, swapping Jev into Recursive Language Model sub-calls was half the cost and 6× faster than Haiku 5.5 on OOLONG at 1M tokens ( @Jnatanh ). Inference Hardware and Serving Systems TPUv7 on AgentX : SemiAnalysis reports 1.42× better perf per dollar than GB300 NVL72 FP4, calculated on an external, non-Google cost basis, and 2.5× versus MI355X ( SemiAnalysis ). Interactivity split : TPUv7 is up to 3.16× better than disaggregated GB200 at medium to high interactivity. GB200 FP4 keeps a 1.2× edge at low interactivity ( thread ). The run was served with vLLM through TorchTPU. Vera Rubin NVL72 on AA-AgentPerf : Up to 5.7× GB300’s throughput per MW on DeepSeek V4 Pro, falling to 2.8× on Kimi K3, with the largest gains at high per-user speed ( AA ). Peak throughput : The gap narrows to 1.14–1.45×. Vera Rubin also posts a record 906 tok/s per user on V4.1 Flash. NVIDIA submitted all of these results. AMD MI355X : 8× MI355X delivers 24.4% more throughput than HGX B300 on Kimi K3 at 50 tok/s per user, and 87.4% more tokens per dollar ( vLLM ). Inferact announced a collaboration with AMD to publish open per-model recipes for agentic serving ( Inferact ).

item.title: Leaked Anthropic Draft AI Regulatory Bill Is Unacceptable and Troubling
item.abstract: There is a newly leaked bill that Anthropic is purportedly shopping around is (if you assume its bugs get fixed). It is similar to the FRONTIER Act, with stronger preemption of state laws, stronger transparency provisions and weaker enforcement provisions. Having slept on this, I find it unacceptable that Anthropic is actively shopping exactly the type of bill I have warned we will need to fight against during the lame duck session. They are trying to use this last time with a Republican Congress to pass preemption of exactly the important state laws, and get some transparency but not much enforcement in exchange. This reads as intentional, that Anthropic is more afraid that the government might enforce rules against Anthropic, than they are worried about the ability of the government to enforce rules against everyone. Anthropic’s policy team seems to have, chosen protecting their business interests and guarding against their political risk, at the expense of safety considerations. There was no need for the company purportedly existing to promote safety to propose a bill that is not even actively stronger than the FRONTIER Act, when the FRONTIER Act was a compromise bill proposed back in June. Even if you were fine with what is being given up, what you get in return very obviously does not meet the moment. Nor is there any need for such compromises. It seems rather insane for Anthropic to be proposing it now. This seems like the bill that someone on the anti-regulatory side should be pushing. It is not obvious this makes us safer than doing nothing, even if the alternative is fully nothing at all levels. Say it isn’t so, Anthropic, or at least that it was a mistake and is no longer so, or I am going to be rather cross. I am at a conference and cannot do an RTFB, but it feels important to get word of this out quickly, especially so Anthropic employees can look into this and ask questions. If you want the full text, here is a copy . I have not had the time to do so, but the other usual suspects quickly sprinted to RTFB (read the bill) and they did not like what they saw. You can try to call this a ‘pretty reasonable AI safety bill’ as Charlie Bullock does, but that is by the standards of people trying to protect the industry from more impactful regulation. POLITICO : Anthropic quietly pitches its own AI safety bill to lawmakers . Ketan Ramakrishnan : Anthropic’s new federal AI bill is, without any overstatement, astonishingly bad. Charlie Bullock : Big news. My take: Anthropic deserves some credit for actually proposing a pretty reasonable AI safety bill; that’s more than other frontier labs have done. But they don’t deserve *too* much credit, IMO; this bill is weaker than the Trahan-Obernolte FRONTIER Act in some key ways, and since the political momentum has shifted significantly in the direction of safety since FRONTIER was introduced back in July, I think new bills introduced today should ideally go further than FRONTIER was able to go rather than regressing. To be fair to Anthropic, the main places where this bill is significantly weaker than FRONTIER are (a) rulemaking (very strong in FRONTIER, almost nonexistent in Anthropic’s bill) and (b) the emergency shutdown authority. Even if you take safety seriously, it might make some sense to dial those authorities back if you didn’t trust the executive branch to wield them responsibly, because those are the easiest provisions for a hypothetical President who hypothetically might not like a certain frontier AI company to abuse. There are some improvements over FRONTIER as well; for instance, this bill does specify that auditors are employed on a continuing basis and has better provisions regarding auditor access to information. Happy to see that from Anthropic (although I think their access provision is still a little undercooked and has Fourth Amendment problems). Overall, I think the embedded auditor bills that get introduced in the coming months are going to be significantly better and more ambitious than this, and I hope Anthropic supports those bills instead of opposing anything that treats catastrophic risks like the serious national security issue they are. Still, it’s encouraging to see a frontier lab come this far. Charlie Bullock : I think the drafting is okay. I’ve seen better but I’ve definitely seen worse. Claude is a pretty good legislative drafter. There are a few clear mistakes but that’s par for the course in a leaked discussion draft. Nathan Calvin : Charlie’s analysis is right but he is nicer than I am – I found myself viscerally angry at multiple points reading this bill. There are some good and sensible parts, but overall this legislation is not remotely close to meeting the moment and I overall think passing it would make us less protected against catastrophic risks than we are under existing law. Two parts that stand out as particularly infuriating when taken together: 1. Some of the preemption provisions are remarkably far reaching and consequential, and in addition to preempting legislation like SB 53 would also remove general powers that state courts have to enjoin defendants and protect the public. Most outrageously, it has a provision that looks like its intended to stops states from enforcing laws or judicial decrees that “suspend the development, deployment, or internal use of an AI model” to protect their citizens from imminent catastrophic harms. Such powers to block and suspend model deployments would then only reside with the federal government. 2. The federal governments powers to restrict the development, deployment, or internal use of a frontier model has to meet an absurdly high bar. First, there needs to be an imminent risk of a catastrophic harm (meaning killing more than 50 people or causing more than a billion dollars in damage). But thats not enough! The agency head needs to make a detailed determination with no deference given to show why no alternative would prevent the imminent catastrophe. Next the court is also explicitly told to consider the harms to the developer and other harms from restricting the model, but no considerations in the other direction. This is absurd! For all of its warning about the potential for AI to cause a catastrophe that kills literally everyone on the planet, Anthropic’s proposed federal law likely makes it harder than under existing law for a court to get an order blocking or restricting the development of frontier models? WTF?? There are also a bunch of others things that I would like to see improved – the substantive details of the auditing section and the potential for rule-making on substantive safety standards both come to mind – but I think these stand out as particularly indefensible. Charlie Bullock : Nathan’s righteous anger has inspired me to make one more mildly disapproving observation: it’s kind of wild that the Anthropic bill has no government licensing for the independent auditors. Licensing is, IMO, the bare minimum thing that you need to even be able to pretend that your auditing regime isn’t just going to devolve into a race to the bottom. Without it, auditors will inevitably compete with each other to offer their customers, the labs, the least bothersome audits available at the lowest possible price point. Obviously Anthropic trusts itself to do a great job of picking great auditors, but do they trust OpenAI to do the same? What about SpaceXSI? The new Anthropic bill is weaker than their June framework, and offers both forward-looking and backward-looking preemption in exchange, despite months of movement to enable us to do more. What are we even doing? Nate Soares : Anthropic’s proposed law would make it even harder than it already is for a court to block or restrict the development of an AI that threatens all humanity. Alex Bores : Anthropic is pitching a bill that closely matches its framework from June.

item.title: Replit is no longer working with Anthropic, CEO says
authors: Kirsten Korosec, Lucas Ropek, Rebecca Bellan
item.abstract: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves. Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s. “Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.” Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027. Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI.
